Content:
I’m a meteorologist.  The weather portion of this is not remotely accurate.  Many problems, but just to start with the first claim about the Appalachians generating storms for NYC -  on the downwind side of a mountain range, the air *descends* rather than rising. If there were mountain-generated storms, they would occur on the upwind face of the mountains, and the downwind area would actually experience a “rain shadow.” Many other problems — almost everything you said about weather was at least mostly incorrect other than “thunderstorms are bad for airports.”
It’s always disappointing when you think a creator does thorough research only to hear them throw out a bunch of plausible sounding BS on a topic you know enough about to realize it’s wrong.

Content: One thing you didn't mention at first, and that not many people have any idea of is that Newark Airport first opened in 1928. Newark airport was the first airport in the NYC metropolitan region, first commercial airport in the nation and first with a paved runway. It also had the first air traffic control tower. It also was the first airport to have night-time departures with lights on the runway in 1953. It was the mayor of Newark at the time who spearheaded the development of the airport. Not the state or the federal government. They picked a site by the seaport, raised it 6ft above the floodplain and that was it. There was no account for the possible future growth and expansion of the airport. It was wedged between a highway (and then 2 with the turnpike being built later) and seaport.

A point hit on, and many of the traveling public don’t realize, is the volume of traffic…planes. 

With continued growth of airlines and business aircraft this leads to a volume problem. 
Only so many planes can fit into a given space. Whether it be the airways, approach corridors, landing slots and the ramp.  Only so many pieces of metal can fit and the entire system is being stretched and stressed.

It’s all about making money and moving money. So follow the money.

Author: @olifrett
Content: Flew out of Newark a few weeks ago (August 2025) for a late afternoon intl flight, 5:30pm, peak thunderstorm moment. I had even received a text earlier that day about potential delays. Flight boarded on time with the looming dark skies over the airport. I could tell there was no way we would leave, yet they still boarded the flight, closed the doors and the thunderstorm hit the airport, lightning, heavy rain, we stayed stuck in the plane, at the gate for 3hrs. Then when it was time to go, there was such a bottleneck on the tarmac, we couldn’t even get out the gate, then a whole musical chairs game for departures on that single open runway, which took an additional 1h30 mins to finally lift off. 4.5 hours. What pissed me off, is that they proceeded with boarding, knowing damn well we weren’t going anywhere and could have postponed it, let passengers linger in the airport, eat, etc and resume smoother departure operations. It was very disorganized. And don’t get me started with security which is understaffed at 4pm for all those 5:30 international flights heading out.

Author: @MarekZBalut
Content: I feel like the catastrophic United delay this year was caused by another issue of American airports, i.e., airlines operating terminals. You said that there was no capacity at the airport, but was it not more likely the case that there was no capacity at Terminal C (the United terminal)? There may have been capacity at other terminals, but because of how the airport works, they simply couldn't go there because none of their people work there. At EWR, Delta and American (among others) share Terminal A, while B is used mostly by foreign airlines. There surely must have been one free place that theoretically could have been used. Last year I left MIA and was struck by how inefficient it all was. There were several flights leaving for Europe at the same time, with passengers for all flights crammed into one area. Meanwhile, the American Airlines gates were empty. Literally not a soul. Apart from that, this was the first time I wondered if these videos are AI produced. The phrase is not "reach" headlines (which was said twice), it's "make" headlines.

It’s not like I’m a native of the area or a UA addict and I do recognize all that I’ve read of complaints from other passengers but, it’s just that I have to take into consideration my personal experience with it. Back in 2001 (all variables equalized) I was 21 and EWR was the third airport I went through in the US (after MIA and ATL) and despite being young, alone and having nothing but guts, good English skills and no fear or shame to ask questions or directions for example, I had zero problem. I arrived at about 5pm and had absolutely no problem to go from gate to baggage claim then train station to Manhattan. I was in NYC for 3 nights then flew to SLC to work in the official vendor of the 2001 Winter Games and, if I’m not wrong, I left out of EWR. No bad recollections there either. Anyways… The longest 5 hours of my life 😂😂😂. That until being cramped in an AA inherited A320 from USAir from FLL to PHX (also 5 hours) where I’d connect to SLC (best snow on earth 😍😍😍). Don’t fly to NYC frequently though. When I do it’s on an international arrival at JFK which is where I leave NYC from.

Content:
I don’t see how weather is really a factor given Philadelphia is exposed to the same weather shenanigans & more intensely so given we get them first and consistently ranks higher, anywhere from 5 to 15ish spots higher in fact. Newark’s abysmal performance is truly down to outdated infrastructure for the quantity of visitors it receives and the congested air within it is forced to operate. The FAA didn’t do it any favors by moving facilities operations here either. Air Traffic Controllers are in high demand EVERYWHERE, across the globe. Demanding relocation was not a wise move, especially considering the majority of those air traffic controllers are likely in their 40s, 50s, or even 60s and nearing retirement. Air Traffic Control is experiencing the same “Silver Tsunami” as every other industry as boomers finally retire and GenX quickly retires on their heels creating a power vacuum that no one is actually prepared to fill in highly skilled, technical jobs because millennials went to traditional college like we were told to, not an aeronautics university for a hyper-specialized degree. 

Oh, and can we then talk about the absolute boner the FAA made by not upgrading infrastructure BEFORE moving the remaining 24 controllers? 

It is genuinely not surprising people are more than happy to take on an Amtrak ticket and come down to Philly for their flights.

Author: @TractControlOff
Content:
My only missed flight to date was during the construction of the new terminal A at EWR (which admittedly is nice) - security took 2.5 hours... at 4am.  Then a 9-hour delay on the rebooked flight.  Then another flight a couple of months later was delayed 10 hours, including 2 hours sitting on a taxiway, then the flight was canceled.  Let's not even discuss the delays in the rebooking line (I left the airport and rebooked... which was 3 days later).  2023 was my worst year in and out of EWR - I believe I had 16 flights delayed (I don't even count a delay if it's less than an hour).  '24 wasn't as brutal but this year has been worse again.  

Advice to anyone flying in/out of EWR: fly early in the day.  Anything after 2pm will be dramatically more prone to significant delays.  Don't connect at EWR unless it's a >2 hour connection and at the same terminal.  Honestly, you'd probably be better off connecting via trains to JFK than EWR some days.  I will say, pre-check/Clear makes a big difference getting through security, at least.

Author: @aribiegeleisen3488
Content:
The timing of this video is funny to me because I was literally just standing in the parking lot of EWR Terminal C, watching planes take off and land, thinking about this exact topic: why this airport is so hated.

Personally, I fly on a bi-weekly basis for business, usually out of Terminal C with United. I have the option to use all three NYC-area airports, and I’ve got to say, I actually prefer Newark over the others.

The parking infrastructure is great. In my experience, the walking time from the parking lot to security, from security to the gate, and even the taxi distance from the gate to the runway is the shortest of all three. In fact, it consistently takes me less than 10 minutes from parking my car to reaching the gate (thanks to touchless ID and PreCheck).

To be fair, I haven’t had any of those nightmare experiences that put Newark in the headlines. Yes, I did avoid it for a few months when they were dealing with major issues, but overall, it's still my top choice to fly out of.

In my opinion, it’s really not as bad as people, or the stats, make it out to be, in real life.

Terminals have been expanded, especially C and a whole new Terminal A, but they can't add any runways to handle the increased traffic.  Newark was never built to become the airport that it is today,

Author: @davidt8087
Content:
Can't stand when non pilots make videos about aviation. Here's a succinct version of why everything here is wrong

1.	The “single crosswind runway” critique is nonsense. Newark (KEWR) has three runways: 4L/22R, 4R/22L, and 11/29. 11/29 is indeed a crosswind runway, but that’s not a “design flaw.” It’s a standard layout—most major airports have a dominant parallel set and one crosswind.
2.	“Runways intersect” — not unusual at all. In fact, hundreds of U.S. airports have intersecting runways (e.g., LAX before the parallels were extended didn’t need it, but places like Boston Logan, Dallas Love, Chicago Midway all have intersects). Newark’s intersecting geometry is normal and safe under FAA rules.
3.	“Runway blocks taxi route” — that’s misleading. At virtually every airport, some taxiways cross runways. That’s why we have hold short points, ground control sequencing, and runway crossing clearances. Calling it a “design flaw” shows a lack of operational knowledge.
4. Aviation isn't all about airliners. Only sim pilots or non pilots constantly believe the piloting world is it just airlines or jets

Author: @cykotronic
Content:
OK… not sure where to start with this. Some of the information is good, but some of it isn’t quite correct. I’m glad you corrected N90’s location, as it’s not in Long Island City but in Westbury, which is a suburb about 13 miles east of NYC proper. I used to do airport capacity planning for the FAA and a regional airport authority, so I’m familiar with EWR. I’ll respond by pointing out specific issues.

EWR layout and operations. Under Visual Flight Rules (basically good weather), the minimum runway separation for simultaneous operations is 700 feet, so EWR’s 900-foot spacing is fine. EWR operates under VFR most of the time. In this case, EWR’s capacity is about 85 movements per hour - roughly 40 landings and 45 departures. This is about average compared to other two-runway airports, even when their parallels are spaced further apart. Plenty of other airports use closely spaced parallels for simultaneous operations - ATL, PHL, ORD, LAX, LAS, etc. Furthermore, most 22R departures start at Taxiway W, which is south of the crosswind runway and doesn’t intersect it at all. And even if the full length were used, it wouldn’t be a big issue since the crosswind runway would function more like a taxiway. Also, it’s not much of a hindrance for arrivals to cross the departure runway. ATC will often wait for a heavy to take off—when the following departure must wait a few minutes due to wake turbulence—and use that gap to cross arrivals. This happens at many busy airports around the country.

Crosswind runway. Believe it or not, the FAA has a configuration where the crosswind runway is used along with the outer parallel for landings. In this case, EWR’s stated capacity is about 100 movements per hour. Airlines used to schedule to that level, which caused delays since ATC mostly stuck with the two parallels. They don’t do this anymore, and the crosswind isn’t used for arrivals now because of airspace and staffing concerns. Still, plenty of other airports use their crosswinds in conjunction with parallels to increase movements - PHL (similar configuration to EWR with an intersecting crosswind), BOS (where nearly all runways crisscross), JFK, ORD (old layout), SFO (intersecting in the middle), LGA (intersecting at the ends), DEN, MEM, etc.

EWR’s seasonal performance. Yes, July is the worst month, mainly because of thunderstorms. However, the airport also has far more flights in July than in February, March, or October, which are the quietest months. In summer, EWR traditionally handled around 1,300 flights a day (fewer now due to FAA scheduling limits). Airlines cut back in the off-peak months, and the airport averaged about 1,050 movements a day. That reduction of 250 flights makes a huge difference in performance. 

N90 EWR sector relocation. A fully staffed EWR sector is around 50 controllers (according to sector controllers I’ve spoken with). Before the move to PHL, they had 33. They sent 24 to PHL (now down to 22), and most of those were on two-year temporary assignments, meaning they’ll return to N90 or elsewhere by next June. From what I’ve heard, they haven’t recruited many new controllers since the move, and none in training are close to certification. It takes about two and a half years to certify, and the fail rate is high because it’s such a complex sector. The FAA’s claim that moving the sector to PHL will improve pass rates is nonsense - PHL tracon is nowhere near as complex, and EWR is still the same, complex sector as before the move. Next summer will be interesting to say the least, as PHL Area C (EWR sector) faces more retirements, and combined with the departure of temporary staff, the airport will be in an even tougher spot. Move has been a complete disaster. 

Equipment issues. These are solely due to the move. The data link set up  was done on the cheap because the FAA was desperate to get the move done quickly. They were warned the equipment set up would be unreliable but didn’t listen. A new, more reliable setup is now in place, but it remains to be seen how well it holds up going forward. It still isn’t a permanent solution.

Right now, EWR is capped at 68 movements an hour. FAA is planning to keep EWR at around this rate for a while. So, there will be slight improvements, but the staffing and potential equipment issues will persist.

Author: @GeoMeridium
Content:
Newark should be next on the USA's airport rebuild list. They have the land footprint to support two independent (1311m+) parallel runways, but the old terminals (frequently rated as the worst in the US) are currently sitting on the footprint of where this new runway would need to be built.

This means that in order to truly address Newark's (and New York City's) capacity issue, all of the terminals (including the Delta one) need to be demolished and rebuilt midfield (in a layout like Shanghai, Seoul, or Atlanta). US 9 would also need to be realigned midfield to maximize space and serve as an access road to the new terminals.

Newark is the only airport in the New York City metro area with the land to truly increase their capacity. LaGuardia and JFK have nowhere to expand/squeeze another independent runway, and Stewart, New Haven, White Plains, and Islip are too far away to be useful, and they lack a true rail transit connection.

Although I support turning the Acela into HSR (and a new terminal-side Acela/MTA station could be a feature of this rebuilt airport), short haul flights don't actually make up a huge percentage of New York metro's air traffic, so that alone won't solve the situation (at least, not without 300mph maglev trains to make trips to Chicago/Atlanta viable).

Author: @stacyp9245
Content:
As a New Jerseyan, who's home airport is EWR/Newark, it's important to remember that:
1- Newark is NJ, not NY for airport classification though it is classified under NY airspace. It split from being an NYC area airport several years back. It is not easy to just transfer to JFK or LGA as NJ transit has had many issues ranging from structural failures (tracks unable to run due to heat causing electricity outages) to staffing shortages (most recently strikes) to damage from storms (downed trees, lines, flooding, etc). The drive from Newark can take an hour minimum to several hours maximum, and costs a lot to get into NYC now due to congesting pricing and bridge tolls. Additionally the other major airport option to defer to is Philadelphia, which has similar issues to being accessed. If you're delayed at Newark, sometimes it takes longer to change flights and airports than waiting it out  (and the cost compounds from having to travel). 
2 - Summer in NJ leads to influxes of tourism due to the shore (Not just NYC visitation), which happens most notably from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day weekend. Coincidentally, our schools let out late June and start early September, which does not help the EWR summer congestions. 
3 - The FAA constraints is 28 flights per hour, which is extremely low, when you're looking at other airport metrics like MSP or LAX. Couple this with our shortages in TSA agents and ATC (who work no more than 2 hour shifts at a time), adds additional time to delays. 

So yes, EWR does suck, but there's so much more that's lost when the nuances are not there to explain the data.

Author: @CrazyPotatos
Content: As a pilot heres a couple more reasons why EWR sucks. The gates are so closely spaced that it takes 5-10 minutes to get off the gate to the point where you can start your engines. Starting engines and getting configured takes another 5 minutes. so 15 minutes after you've "left" you've made it a few hundred feet, and thats not accounting for any traffic. Then you go wait in line, and learn they've stopped/delayed departures for... reasons. Often they state weather, which is the industry's get out of jail free card. We can't control the weather so anytime anything to do with aviation has any delays we blame weather, even though its often not a big problem. The problem is that ATC is not equipped to handle weather deviations in the surrounding airspace. New York Approach and Center control such a small sliver of airspace that any deviations outside of their airspace require coordination with other facitilies which increases controller workload and therefore reduces how much traffic one controller can handle. Additionally, all NY airports departure procedures require vectors to your flightplan. This requires controllers to make more radio calls (reducing one controllers capacity) to get airplanes to their flight planned route, instead of just having RNAV sids that connect to enroute fixes. Its a giant mess, nothing has been done about it for years, and I avoid flying over there because of it.
